root_cause.text: `tmigr_handle_remote_cpu()` in `kernel/time/timer_migration.c` incorrectly skipped `timer_expire_remote()` for the local CPU, assuming the local softirq path had already expired its timers, but `jiffies` could advance between `run_timer_base(BASE_GLOBAL)` and the remote expiry check, leaving an expired timer on the wheel and causing the hierarchical timer migration loop to livelock.
root_cause.evidence: The patch removes `if (cpu != smp_processor_id())` and adds a comment explaining that “jiffies might have advanced after the timer softirq invoked run_timer_base(BASE_GLOBAL) and the point where the jiffies snapshot @jif was taken,” while the CVE description says the timer is “ignored,” “the callback is never invoked and removed,” and `fetch_next_timer_interrupt_remote()` keeps re-queuing it with `expires == now`, making the `goto-again` loop spin indefinitely.

intent_record.intent_summary: Always expire the remote timer after unlocking, fixing a race where the local CPU could incorrectly skip expiration due to a stale jiffies comparison.
intent_record.what: The conditional check `if (cpu != smp_processor_id())` guarding `timer_expire_remote(cpu);` was removed, and a comment was added explaining why the call must now be unconditional.
intent_record.how: After releasing `tmc->lock`, `timer_expire_remote(cpu)` will be invoked for both remote and local CPUs. This ensures timer expiration is not skipped when the local CPU's jiffies have advanced between the timer softirq snapshot and the later handling path, preventing a missed remote timer expiration in that race.

grouping_result.intent: Always expire the remote timer after unlocking, fixing a race where the local CPU could incorrectly skip expiration due to a stale jiffies comparison.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it fixes the local-CPU path in tmigr_handle_remote_cpu() so remote timer expiration is always performed after unlocking, avoiding the stale jiffies check that could skip timer_expire_remote() and leave an expired timer on the wheel.

candidates.rationale: This conditional is the direct cause of the bug: it skips timer_expire_remote() on the local CPU based on a stale CPU comparison, which can leave an expired timer on the wheel and trigger the livelock described in the root cause.

vuln_statements.explanation: This condition incorrectly skips the remote timer expiration path when the target CPU is the local CPU. As described in the root cause, that assumption can be stale because jiffies may advance between the global timer run and the remote expiry check, leaving an expired timer on the wheel and causing the migration loop to livelock.

bic_trace_step.reason: The shown code is sufficient to assess the specific issue in this commit because it includes the complete implementation of `tmigr_handle_remote_cpu()` and the surrounding remote-expiry logic. The vulnerable construct described in the root cause is not present here: this function explicitly avoids the problematic early-skip behavior by only returning early for genuinely inapplicable cases: `if (!tmc->online || tmc->remote || tmc->cpuevt.ignore || now < tmc->cpuevt.nextevt.expires) { ... return; }`. Crucially, when the CPU is the target of remote expiry and may still have work after the local base walk, the code sets `tmc->remote = true;`, drops the lock, and later re-enters the hierarchy update path after fetching remote timer state: `fetch_next_timer_interrupt_remote(jif, now, &tevt, cpu); ... data.remote = true; ... walk_groups(&tmigr_new_timer_up, &data, tmc);`. The fix for the reported livelock is already reflected in the added logic that performs the hierarchy update even when there is no new global timer pending: `"The update is done even when there is no 'new' global timer pending on the remote CPU"`. There is no code path here that skips `timer_expire_remote()` specifically for the local CPU due to an assumption that the local softirq path already expired its timers; instead, remote handling is guarded by `if (cpu != smp_processor_id()) timer_expire_remote(cpu);`, which only omits the call when processing the current CPU itself. Therefore the vulnerable construct is absent and the commit already contains the corrected handling.
